draft.title: Internment of enemy aliens
card: An enemy alien was a person living in a country at war with the country of their birth or background. In Australia, people of German, Italian and Japanese background were seen this way.
Many of them were suspected of being a possible danger to Australia. This was often based on their background, not on anything they had done.
Internment means holding people in a camp without a trial. Thousands of people in Australia were held in internment camps during the war.
Some of those interned had lived in Australia for years, and some families were separated.
draft.remember: Thousands of people were interned because of their German, Italian or Japanese background.

a.q: Why were many people in Australia held in internment camps in WWII?
opts: Their background linked them to an enemy country
They had refused to join the Australian army
They had been tried and found guilty of spying
They had broken government rationing rules
a.why: People of German, Italian and Japanese background were seen as enemy aliens because of the countries they came from. Many were held without a trial, so a guilty verdict for spying is wrong.
a.clue: Think about where they or their families came from.

b.q: Marco came to Australia from Italy years before the war and ran a fruit shop in Perth. In 1940 he was taken to a camp. What does this show about internment?
opts: People could be interned because of their background
Only people who had been caught spying were interned
Only people who had just arrived in Australia were interned
Internment was only for people of Japanese background
b.why: Marco had lived in Australia for years and was held because he was of Italian background, which shows that background could be enough. The idea that only spies were held is wrong, because many people were held without a trial.
b.clue: Look at why Marco was taken, not what he did.

a.best: Their background linked them to an enemy country

b.best: People could be interned because of their background

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('could'), while all three wrong options use 'only'. A student can pick the answer by spotting the absolutes, without knowing the idea.
The clue 'Think about where they or their families came from' points straight to the only option about background, so it gives the answer away.
The clue 'Look at why Marco was taken, not what he did' rules out every option about actions, which leaves only the background option. It gives the answer away.

The remember line says the thousands were interned because of their background. The card says suspicion was 'often' based on background, so the remember line states the cause more absolutely than the card does.

The why's reasoning is weak. Being held without a trial does not by itself show that people were not spies. It would be clearer to say that Marco had done nothing wrong and was held for his background.

a.q: What did it mean for an enemy alien in Australia to be interned in WWII?
opts: Being held in a camp without a trial
Being held in a prison after a trial
Being sent back to their country of birth
Being made to pay a fine to the government
a.why: Internment meant being held in a camp without a trial. Being held after a trial is wrong, because internment did not need a court to find a person guilty of anything.

b.q: Marco came to Australia from Italy years before the war and ran a fruit shop in Perth. He had broken no laws. In 1940 he was taken to a camp. What does his case show could lead to internment?
opts: An Italian background, even after years living here
A conviction for spying, after a trial in court
Arriving in Australia only a short time before
Refusing to do the war work the government set
b.why: Marco had lived in Australia for years and had done nothing wrong, yet he was held in a camp. His Italian background was enough. A spying conviction does not fit, because Marco broke no laws and internment did not need a trial.
b.clue: Check each option against the facts given about Marco.
